name: Denmark
traditionNote: A Nordic system with light codification: there is no civil code, contract and tort law rest on old statutes and case law together, and the forarbejder — the bill's explanatory remarks and the committee report — are read as a matter of course when a provision is unclear.
summary: An act (lov) is passed by the Folketing in three readings, signed by the Monarch and a minister, and published in Lovtidende — publication being the condition of its taking effect. Executive rules come as bekendtgørelser issued by a minister under an authorisation in an act, and internal instructions as cirkulærer and vejledninger; all appear in Lovtidende or, for the softer instruments, in the state legal information system. Since 2008 Lovtidende has been published only electronically, and the electronic edition is the authentic one. Denmark has no constitutional court: the ordinary courts review statutes against the Grundlov in ordinary cases, and have struck one down exactly once. The Kingdom is not only Denmark: the Faroe Islands and Greenland are self-governing parts of it, each with its own legislature and its own gazette, and Danish acts do not extend to them unless made applicable by royal decree.
hierarchy: Danmarks Riges Grundlov (Constitutional Act of 5 June 1953)
EU law, applied with primacy since accession in 1973, subject to the limits the Supreme Court set in the Maastricht and Ajos cases
Lov — acts of the Folketing, including the acts incorporating the European Convention on Human Rights
Anordninger — royal decrees, including the decrees that put Danish acts into force in Greenland or the Faroe Islands
Bekendtgørelse — ministerial orders issued under a statutory authorisation
Cirkulære, vejledning and skrivelse — instructions binding the administration internally
Kommunale regulativer og vedtægter — municipal rules under the Local Government Act, published locally

gazette.name: Lovtidende
gazette.coverage: Acts, royal decrees, ministerial orders and treaties; electronic-only publication since 2008, when the printed edition ceased
gazette.desc: The gazette that makes a Danish rule effective. Publication here is not a formality — an act or an order that has not been published in Lovtidende cannot be applied — and since 2008 the electronic edition is the authentic one, with no paper version behind it.
gazette.howto: Browse or search the documents section by year, type and issuing ministry; each item carries its Lovtidende reference, the date of publication and a signed PDF. For the consolidated text of the same rule, cross over to Retsinformation, which is the searchable system built on this material.
gazette.note: Lovtidende C carried treaties and is now folded into the same electronic publication; older treaty items are cited as LTC with year and number.

constitution.name: Danmarks Riges Grundlov
constitution.native: Danmarks Riges Grundlov (lov nr. 169 af 5. juni 1953)
constitution.authority: Adopted by referendum and signed 5 June 1953; published as act no. 169 of that date
constitution.coverage: In force since 5 June 1953, unamended since; the Act of Succession was changed by referendum in 2009 without touching the constitutional text
constitution.desc: A short constitution, unchanged for over seventy years, in which the courts' power to review legislation is nowhere written down and has nonetheless been exercised — once successfully, in the Tvind case of 1999. Section 20, on transferring powers to international authorities, is the provision that carried Danish EU membership and is the one most litigated.
constitution.howto: Read the text on Retsinformation, addressed by its European Legislation Identifier; the Folketing publishes an English translation, 'My Constitutional Act', on its own site.
constitution.note: Amendment is deliberately near-impossible: both chambers of the same Folketing before and after an election, then a referendum in which the yes votes must be at least forty per cent of the whole electorate.

sources.name: Retsinformation
sources.coverage: All acts, ministerial orders and circulars in force, with consolidated versions (lovbekendtgørelser); Folketing bills and reports; and the Ombudsman's published statements
sources.desc: The single entry point to Danish law in force. Its distinctive Danish feature is the lovbekendtgørelse: rather than maintaining an editorial consolidation, the responsible ministry periodically republishes the whole act as an official consolidated text with a new number, and that text is itself published in Lovtidende.
sources.howto: Search under 'Regler' for legislation, 'Afgørelser' for decisions and 'Lov- og beslutningsforslag' for bills, or pick a ministry and narrow from there. Documents are addressed by ELI — retsinformation.dk/eli/lta/1953/169 — and the API is documented on the site. Check whether you are reading a lovbekendtgørelse and, if so, whether anything has amended it since.
sources.note: A lovbekendtgørelse is official but is a snapshot: amendments passed after it appear as separate acts and are not merged until the next one is issued.

sources.name: Domsdatabasen
sources.coverage: Judgments of the Supreme Court, the two high courts and the district courts, published progressively since the database opened in 2022 and building forward rather than backward
sources.desc: Denmark's first free public case-law database, and a recent one: before it, Danish judgments were effectively available only through the commercial services and the printed Ugeskrift for Retsvæsen. Coverage grows from its start date, so it is thin for older material by design.
sources.howto: Search by court, date, case number or subject; judgments are anonymised under the rules the Court Administration publishes alongside the database. For older decisions, the printed Ugeskrift for Retsvæsen and the subscription services remain the route.
sources.note: Not retrospective. A decision's absence tells you when the database began, not whether the case exists.

sources.name: Folketinget
sources.coverage: Bills and resolutions with their three readings, committee reports and questions, the record of proceedings, and the parliamentary year's documents by session
sources.desc: Where a Danish act is followed while it is a bill, and where its preparatory works are. The bemærkninger — the explanatory remarks printed with the bill, general and section by section — are the standard material for interpreting the resulting provision, and the committee's betænkning records what changed and why.
sources.howto: Find the bill by its L number and session, then read the remarks and the committee report; the same documents are mirrored in Retsinformation's bills section. The EU information service, eu-oplysningen.dk, tracks the EU side of the Folketing's work.
sources.note: The site answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.

sources.name: Statstidende
sources.coverage: Legally required notices — probate, insolvency, compulsory sales, summonses, company and public-procurement notices — published daily and archived
sources.desc: The notice gazette, distinct from Lovtidende: no legislation, but the announcements from which legal deadlines run. A creditor's claim period in a bankruptcy or an estate begins with the notice published here.
sources.howto: Search by type of notice, name or date, or subscribe to a search so that new matching notices are pushed to you; the archive is open and free.
sources.note: Publication here has legal consequences but never creates a rule. Do not confuse it with Lovtidende.

sources.name: Folketingets Ombudsmand
sources.authority: Folketingets Ombudsmand, elected by the Folketing
sources.coverage: Published statements on complaints and own-initiative cases, the annual report, the Ombudsman's overview of administrative law (Myndighedsguiden), and monitoring visits to institutions
sources.desc: The working authority on Danish administrative law. Because so few administrative disputes reach the courts, the Ombudsman's statements — on reasons, case-handling times, access to documents, impartiality — are in practice where the standards are set, and Myndighedsguiden states them systematically.
sources.howto: Search the statements by subject, authority or year; the numbering is by year and running number. Statements are also indexed in Retsinformation, which lets you find them from the provision they concern.
sources.note: The Ombudsman cannot annul a decision or bind a court; the influence is persuasive, and considerable.

sources.name: Logasavnid (Faroe Islands)
sources.authority: Løgmansskrivstovan (Prime Minister's Office of the Faroe Islands)
sources.coverage: Faroese legislation in force and historical, including løgtingslógir, kunngerðir, and the Danish acts and royal decrees that apply in the islands
sources.desc: The Faroe Islands legislate for themselves in every field taken over under the home rule and takeover arrangements, and Danish acts reach the islands only through an anordning made for them. This collection holds both halves, which is why its filter for type of instrument lists Faroese and Danish forms side by side.
sources.howto: Use the search with the filters for status (galdandi for in force, áður galdandi for formerly in force, søgulig for historical), for the responsible ministry and for the type of instrument — løgtingslóg, kunngerð, anordning, lov, bekendtgørelse. The companion Kunngerðasavnið holds the published gazette items.
sources.note: Faroese law is in Faroese; the Danish instruments applying there are in Danish. Neither is translated into English by the authorities.

sources.name: Nalunaarutit (Greenland)
sources.coverage: Inatsisartut acts and Naalakkersuisut orders, together with the Danish acts and royal decrees in force for Greenland
sources.desc: Greenland has taken over most fields of law under the Self-Government Act of 2009, and its parliament, the Inatsisartut, legislates in them; Danish legislation applies only where a royal decree puts it into force there. This portal is where both are published, in Greenlandic and Danish.
sources.howto: Search by year, number and type, or browse by subject; the site is served in Danish and Greenlandic through the language switch. The Inatsisartut's own site at ina.gl carries the bills and the record of debates.
sources.note: Criminal law and the administration of justice in Greenland run on a separate Danish criminal code and administration of justice act written specifically for Greenland, not on the mainland ones.

sources.name: EU-Oplysningen
sources.coverage: Explanations of EU law and institutions, the treaties in Danish, and the Folketing's scrutiny of EU proposals through its European Affairs Committee
sources.desc: Denmark's parliamentary scrutiny of EU legislation is unusually strong — the European Affairs Committee gives the government a negotiating mandate — and this service documents both the substance of EU law in Danish and how that scrutiny works.
sources.howto: Use the topic pages for an explanation and the treaty texts, and the committee pages for what the Folketing has been asked to mandate; for the legal texts themselves, cross to EUR-Lex in Danish.
sources.note: Explanatory material produced by a parliamentary service, not a source of law.

sources.name: EUR-Lex (pa dansk)
sources.authority: Den Europæiske Unions Publikationskontor (Publications Office of the European Union)
sources.coverage: EU treaties, legislation, consolidated texts, case law and national implementing measures, in Danish among the official languages
sources.desc: Retsinformation carries no EU legislation, and since 1973 a substantial part of what applies in Denmark is an EU regulation that required no Danish act. Denmark's opt-outs mean the coverage is not uniform: justice and home affairs in particular applies to Denmark only in part.
sources.howto: Search by CELEX number or subject with the interface set to Danish; the national implementing measures tab on a directive lists the Danish acts and orders notified for it. Check whether an instrument is caught by a Danish opt-out before assuming it applies.
sources.note: The Danish language version of an EU act is authentic alongside the others; the Official Journal edition is the binding one. Neither the Faroe Islands nor Greenland is in the EU.

sources.name: The Constitutional Act in English (Folketinget)
sources.en: The Constitutional Act of Denmark in English
sources.coverage: The full constitutional text in English, published as a booklet and as a PDF, with explanatory material alongside it
sources.desc: The Folketing's own English edition of the Constitutional Act, with commentary written for a general reader — effectively the only Danish constitutional material the state publishes in English.
sources.howto: The page carries the text and links the PDF edition, the-constitutional-act-of-denmark.pdf, under Publications; the Danish text on Retsinformation is what any wording must be checked against.
sources.note: A translation, with no legal force. Danish statutes generally are not translated by the state. The parliament's English site answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.

sources.name: Karnov
sources.coverage: Annotated legislation, the case-law archive including Ugeskrift for Retsvæsen, commentary and practice material
sources.desc: The service Danish practice runs on, and the holder of Ugeskrift for Retsvæsen, the reports series in which Danish judgments have been cited for well over a century. Its notes to each provision are the closest thing Denmark has to a general commentary.
sources.howto: Access requires a subscription or an institutional login. The free public sources cover legislation and recent judgments; what the subscription buys is the annotation and the historical case law.
sources.note: Private and commercial. A UfR citation refers to its reports, not to a public database.

sources.name: Hojesteret
sources.coverage: The Court's recent judgments and orders with summaries, its hearing list, and its rules on leave to appeal
sources.desc: The final instance for civil and criminal cases, sitting since 1661 and never as a constitutional court — it reviews statutes against the Grundlov only when deciding an ordinary case, and has held a statute unconstitutional once, in 1999. Appeal to it normally requires leave from the Appeals Permission Board.
sources.howto: Read the summaries of recent decisions on the Court's pages and follow into the full text; for anything older, use the public judgments database from 2022 onward and Ugeskrift for Retsvæsen before that.
sources.note: The site answers automated requests with 403 while serving browsers normally.

sources.name: Ankestyrelsen — principafgorelser
sources.en: National Social Appeals Board, principle decisions
sources.coverage: Principle decisions on social, employment and child welfare law, and the Board's practice notes, published continuously
sources.desc: Included because in Denmark the appeals boards, not the courts, decide most of the law that touches individuals directly. A principafgørelse of the Board binds the municipalities in later cases of the same kind, which makes it operative law in a way that a court judgment on the same question rarely gets to be.
sources.howto: Search the principle decisions by subject and year; each states the provisions applied and the rule it settles. They are also indexed in Retsinformation, so they can be reached from the provision they interpret.
sources.note: Binding on the administration, not on the courts. A court can and occasionally does take a different view.

findLaw.task: Find the current text of an act
findLaw.steps: Search Retsinformation for the act and take the most recent lovbekendtgørelse — the officially republished consolidated version — then check whether any act published after it has amended it. Both the consolidation and the amendments have their own Lovtidende numbers.

Open Lovtidende and find the item by year, type and ministry; the signed PDF is the authentic text and its publication date is what entry into force runs from. An order that never appeared here cannot be applied against you.

findLaw.task: Find the ministerial order under an act
findLaw.steps: Most Danish detail is in a bekendtgørelse. Search Retsinformation filtered to that ministry, or work from the act's authorising section; the order states the provision it is made under, and an order that exceeds it is invalid.

Search the public judgments database by court, date or case number; it starts in 2022 and grows forward, so older decisions are found instead through Ugeskrift for Retsvæsen and the commercial services. Supreme Court judgments are cited by date and case number.

findLaw.task: Work out what a provision was meant to do
findLaw.steps: Find the bill on the Folketing site by its L number and session and read the bemærkninger — the explanatory remarks, both general and section by section — then the committee's betænkning for what changed during passage. Danish courts use these routinely.

findLaw.task: Check how an authority is supposed to behave
findLaw.steps: Look for the Ombudsman's statements on the point and at Myndighedsguiden, the systematic account of administrative law. Case-handling times, reasons, partiality and access to documents are settled here far more often than in court.

findLaw.task: Find law that applies in the Faroe Islands or Greenland
findLaw.steps: Do not assume a Danish act applies. Check the Faroese collection or the Greenland portal for the local act on the subject, and for a Danish act check whether a royal decree has put it into force there. Both jurisdictions legislate for themselves in the fields they have taken over.

subnational: The Kingdom of Denmark has three parts and only one of them is governed by the Danish corpus alone. The Faroe Islands, under home rule since 1948 and the takeover act of 2005, legislate through the Løgting in every field they have assumed, publishing løgtingslógir and kunngerðir in the Faroese collection; Greenland, under the Self-Government Act of 2009, legislates through the Inatsisartut and publishes in Greenlandic and Danish on its own portal. In both, a Danish act applies only if a royal decree — an anordning — has been issued putting it into force there, usually with adaptations, and neither is part of the EU. Within Denmark proper there is no legislating tier below the state: the 98 municipalities and five regions adopt regulativer, vedtægter and charges under powers granted by act, published by the municipality itself and gathered in no national database, and their legality is tested by the state supervisory authority rather than by a constitutional route.
caveats: Denmark's consolidated texts work differently from most: a lovbekendtgørelse is an official republication issued at a point in time, not a continuously maintained text, so the current wording is that document plus every amending act published since. Publication in Lovtidende is constitutive — an unpublished order cannot be applied — and since 2008 there is no paper edition behind the electronic one. The free judgments database began only in 2022 and does not go back, so for older case law the printed Ugeskrift for Retsvæsen and the commercial services are still the route, and Danish citation practice reflects that. There is no constitutional court and judicial review of statutes has succeeded once in the history of the 1953 Act, so 'unconstitutional' is a much weaker claim in Denmark than in most of Europe. EU law does not apply uniformly because of the Danish opt-outs. And the Kingdom is not one legal area: assuming a Danish act extends to the Faroe Islands or Greenland is the most common mistake made about Danish law.
